chunks: From them, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fazzal, from Ali ibn Uqba and Tha'labah ibn Maymun and Ghalib ibn Uthman and Harun ibn Muslim, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya, who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) in his tent at Mina. He looked at Ziyad al-Aswad, whose leg was swollen/inflamed, and pitied him. He said to him, 'What is the matter with your legs that they are like this?' He said, 'I came upon a weak mount (donkey), so I walked for most of the way.'

He pitied him, and at that time Ziyad said to him, 'I am afflicted by sins to the extent that when I thought I was destroyed, I remembered my love for you, and I hoped for salvation, and clarity/lightness came to me.'
So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'And is the Religion anything except for love?'
He made faith lovely to you and adorned it in your hearts
And He said, 'If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you'
And He said, 'They love those who have migrated to them'

Indeed, a man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I love those who pray but I do not pray, and I love those who fast but I do not fast.' The Messenger of Allah said to him, 'You are with the one whom you love, and for you is what you have acquired.'

And he (peace be upon him) said, 'What you seek and what you desire: Indeed, if there were a scare from the sky, every people would flee to their place of safety, and we would flee to our Prophet, and you would flee to us.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of love (hub) in Shia theology according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in Al-Kafi, highlights the theological centrality of 'Hubb' (love) in Shia jurisprudence, where Ziyad al-Aswad’s physical exertion is framed as a spiritual act of devotion. Abu Ja'far al-Baqir (as) validates this by linking personal piety to the emotional bond with the Ahl al-Bayt, citing Quranic verses that characterize believers by their love for the Prophet and the Emigrants. The narration concludes with the eschatological principle that the Imams serve as the ultimate sanctuary ('ma'man') for their followers on the Day of Judgment, reinforcing the concept of intercession and refuge.
